Hungary is not considered highly exposed, but it is not earthquake-free either. The national seismological network records on average 100–120 smaller earthquakes (below magnitude 2.5) a year, most of which cannot be felt; four or five a year are clearly felt around the epicentre but do not yet cause damage. An earthquake causing more significant damage occurs every 15–20 years, and a strong one causing very heavy damage (M 5.5–6.0) every 40–50 years. The first known earthquake in Hungary occurred on 7 September 456 in Savaria, near today’s Szombathely (M ≈ 6.1). The area stretching from Komárom to the northern end of Lake Balaton is still one of the most active parts of the country; in the east, near the Hungarian–Romanian border, the activity of the Érmellék seismic zone has been known since 1829 – the damage from the 1834 earthquake can still be seen in the church of Máriapócs.
Rainwater must be drained away and leaking utility pipes repaired: soaking is the main cause of failure.

Urban tunnelling is also cavity excavation: behind the shield tunnelling machine, because of the gap between the lining ring and the soil and the movement of the soil ahead of the face, a settlement trough travels along the tunnel alignment at the surface. The shape of the trough is well approximated by a Gaussian curve: the maximum settlement is above the tunnel axis, and the inflection point, where the trough is steepest, lies at a distance i = K·z0 from the axis. The volume of the trough can be calculated from the volume loss (a few tenths of a per cent of the tunnel cross-section) – for modern closed-face shields it is typically 0.3–0.5 %.

Flowing water exerts a seepage force on the soil skeleton in the direction of flow, proportional to the hydraulic gradient (i = Δh/L, the fall in water level per unit length of flow path). For upward flow, at the critical gradient, icr = γ′/γw ≈ 1, the effective stress drops to zero: the soil loses its weight and behaves like a dense liquid – this is a boil, “quicksand”. A much smaller gradient is enough to wash the fine grains out of a loose skeleton (suffusion) – especially in gap-graded soils, and in uniform fine sand and silt.

One consideration in choosing the foundation level is that the footing should lie below the frost depth. In Hungarian practice the frost depth is 0.8 m in fine-grained soil, and 1.0 m above 500 m above Baltic sea level. In coarse-grained soil it is also 0.8 m, but below 500 m it may be reduced to 0.5 m if the winter groundwater level stays at least 2.0 m below the foundation level. The depth of frost penetration depends on the severity and duration of the frost (the freezing index) and on the thermal conductivity and water content of the soil: in wet soil the latent heat of the freezing water slows the frost front.
